Which one of the following correctly matches a plane of movement with its paired axis?
A) Sagittal plane — sagittal axis
B) Frontal plane — frontal axis
C) Transverse plane — vertical axis
D) Sagittal plane — vertical axis
practice_questions.marks: C) Transverse plane — vertical axis [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify the plane of movement and the axis of rotation when a gymnast performs a front somersault.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for sagittal plane; 1 mark for frontal axis (also accept transverse/mediolateral axis).

practice_questions.text: Describe the movement of a trampolinist performing a full twist jump, using the correct terms for the plane and axis involved.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: transverse plane (1); vertical axis / longitudinal axis (1); the body rotates horizontally around the long axis from head to toe, spinning left or right (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a gymnast tucks their body tightly during a somersault.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: the somersault occurs in the sagittal plane around the frontal axis (1); tucking brings the body mass closer to the axis of rotation (1); this increases the speed of rotation, allowing the gymnast to complete more rotations before landing (1).

practice_questions.text: A dance teacher is analysing the movement patterns of students performing a routine that includes a cartwheel, a forward roll and a full spin. Analyse the planes and axes involved in each movement and explain how this understanding could help the teacher correct technique.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correctly identifies all three plane-axis pairings: cartwheel in frontal plane around sagittal axis; forward roll in sagittal plane around frontal axis; full spin in transverse plane around vertical axis. Explains application to teaching: understanding which plane a movement is in tells the teacher whether the error is in forward/backward, side-to-side or rotational direction; correcting a cartwheel error (sagittal axis rotation) requires different cues than correcting a somersault (frontal axis). Technically precise throughout with consistent teaching application.

Secure: Identifies at least two of three pairings correctly. Connects plane-axis analysis to correcting technique in a sporting context.

Developing: Identifies one or two plane-axis pairings with some errors. Limited application to teaching.

Emerging: Names one plane or axis. No or minimal application.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the usefulness of the planes and axes framework for a coach analysing and improving a competitive swimmer's tumble turn technique.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: For — the framework precisely identifies which planes are involved in each phase of the tumble turn (e.g. forward rotation into the wall is sagittal plane around frontal axis; any body twist is transverse plane around vertical axis). This specificity allows the coach to isolate technique errors by plane, set drill progressions that isolate one rotational direction at a time, and communicate corrections in precise anatomical language. Against — the framework has limitations: it does not account for force, speed or timing; a swimmer who understands the planes might still have poor muscle recruitment or coordination; the framework is analytical, not prescriptive. Conclusion: the framework is highly useful as a diagnostic tool but must be combined with biomechanical and physiological analysis for full coaching effectiveness. Balanced, applied, concluded.

Secure: Identifies advantages and at least one limitation. Swimming application present. Attempted conclusion.

Developing: Discusses benefits with limited limitations. Partial sporting context.

Emerging: Basic description of one plane. No evaluation.

lessons.title: Health, Fitness and Components of Fitness

before.description: Health, fitness, exercise and performance defined, plus the ten components needed for sport.
before.content_html:
Health and Fitness: Not the Same Thing

Most people use the words “healthy” and “fit” interchangeably, but in sports science they have precise, separate definitions. Health is defined as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being — not simply the absence of illness. A person can feel stressed, anxious or socially isolated and still have no diagnosable disease, meaning their health is compromised even if a doctor finds nothing wrong.

Fitness, in contrast, is defined as the ability to meet the demands of the environment. This makes fitness specific to purpose: a sprinter needs explosive power and speed; a marathon runner needs cardiovascular endurance; a goalkeeper needs agility and reaction time. A person who is highly fit for one sport may be relatively unfit for another.

Two further definitions complete the picture. Exercise is any form of physical activity that maintains or improves health and fitness — it is a subset of physical activity that has a deliberate fitness aim. Performance refers to how effectively a person executes a skill or task during physical activity or competition. All four concepts — health, fitness, exercise and performance — are distinct but closely related: regular exercise improves fitness, which supports both health and performance.

Key Fact

Four key definitions: Health = complete physical, mental and social well-being. Fitness = ability to meet demands of the environment. Exercise = physical activity that maintains or improves health/fitness. Performance = how well a person executes a skill in sport. Being fit does not automatically mean being healthy, and vice versa.

Health-Related Components of Fitness

The ten components of fitness are divided into two groups. The health-related components are those most directly linked to a person’s physical health and ability to resist lifestyle diseases. There are five:

Cardiovascular endurance (also called aerobic endurance) is the ability of the heart, lungs and circulatory system to supply oxygen to working muscles over a sustained period. Distance runners, rowers and cyclists have very high cardiovascular endurance. Strength is the maximum force a muscle or group of muscles can exert in a single effort against a resistance. A rugby prop in a scrum relies heavily on strength. Muscular endurance is the ability of a muscle or group of muscles to sustain repeated contractions against a resistance for an extended period — a rower completing a 2,000-metre race or a cyclist climbing a hill over many minutes both need muscular endurance. Flexibility is the range of movement possible at a joint. Gymnasts require extreme flexibility across multiple joints. Body composition is the ratio of fat mass to lean mass (muscle, bone and organs) in the body. A healthy body composition supports both performance and long-term health.

Skill-Related Components of Fitness

The skill-related components are those that primarily affect the quality of sporting performance rather than general health. There are five:

Agility is the ability to change direction quickly and accurately while maintaining control. A rugby winger sidestepping a defender or a tennis player changing court position both rely on agility. Balance is the ability to maintain the body’s centre of mass over its base of support, either statically (standing still) or dynamically (moving). A gymnast performing a handstand uses static balance; a surfer uses dynamic balance.

Coordination is the ability to use different body parts together in a smooth, accurate and controlled way. A cricket batsman hitting a ball requires the coordination of eyes, hands and body rotation. Power is the ability to exert maximum muscular force in the shortest possible time — it combines strength and speed. A sprinter leaving the starting blocks and a discus thrower generating release velocity both rely on power. Reaction time is the time taken to detect a stimulus and initiate a response. A swimmer diving off the blocks in response to the starting signal, or a goalkeeper reacting to a penalty kick, both rely on short reaction times.

Finally, speed is the ability to move the body or a limb quickly from one point to another. A 100 m sprinter requires maximum running speed; a fast bowler in cricket needs arm speed to generate ball velocity.

Key Fact

Health-related: cardiovascular endurance, strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, body composition. Skill-related: agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time, speed. Most sports require a combination of both groups — a basketball player needs cardiovascular endurance (health-related) and agility and coordination (skill-related).

When a question asks you to link components of fitness to a sport, you must justify the choice. Saying “a footballer needs speed” earns half the marks; saying “a footballer needs speed to chase a through-ball and get to it before the defender” earns full marks. For each component you name, follow the pattern: name the component, identify when in the sport it is needed, and explain how it affects performance. Mark schemes reward the link between the component and the sporting context, not just the component name alone.

A common misconception is that a very fit person is automatically healthy, or that an unhealthy person cannot be fit. The two are related but distinct. An elite gymnast may have excellent flexibility, cardiovascular endurance and body composition (very fit) but suffer from disordered eating or stress-related injury (compromised health). Conversely, a person with a diagnosed chronic condition such as controlled diabetes may score below norms on fitness tests but maintain good mental and social well-being (reasonably healthy). Recognising this distinction is important for exam questions that ask you to compare or contrast the two concepts.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Health (complete physical, mental and social well-being) and fitness (ability to meet the demands of the environment) are distinct concepts; being fit does not automatically mean being healthy.
  • The five health-related components are cardiovascular endurance, strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition. The five skill-related components are agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time and speed.
  • Matching components to a sport requires justification — name the component, identify when it is used, and explain how it improves performance.

before.exam_tip_html: For data interpretation questions, follow the three-step rule that examiners reward: (1) quote a specific figure with units from the data, (2) make a comparison or identify a trend (e.g. compare to normative data or a previous result), (3) state the sporting or training implication. Simply writing “the score increased” without a number, or writing a number without a comparison, each lose a mark. For calculation questions involving percentage improvement, always show the formula, then the substitution, then the final answer with a percentage sign. On questions asking you to select the most appropriate fitness test for a sport, you must justify your choice by linking the test to the relevant component of fitness required in that sport.
before.content_html:
Why Fitness Testing Matters

Fitness testing gives coaches and athletes a precise picture of current physical condition. Without measurement, training decisions rely on guesswork. With structured testing, a coach can identify which components of fitness are strengths and which need attention, establish a baseline from which improvement is tracked, compare results against national norms, and motivate athletes with concrete targets. There are several reasons to carry out fitness tests: to identify strengths and weaknesses, to monitor improvement over time, to establish a starting level of fitness, to inform training requirements, to compare results against norms or previous personal bests, and to motivate athletes and help them set realistic goals.

Key Fact

Six reasons for fitness testing: (1) identify strengths and weaknesses, (2) monitor improvement, (3) establish a baseline, (4) inform training needs, (5) compare to norms, (6) motivate and set realistic goals. In the exam, giving just one reason earns only part marks — learn the full list.

Cardiovascular Endurance Tests

Three tests assess cardiovascular endurance. The Cooper 12-minute run test requires the participant to run as far as possible in 12 minutes on a flat, measured course. The distance covered is recorded and compared against age and gender normative tables. The Cooper 12-minute swim test follows the same principle in the water. The Harvard Step Test (school-adapted GCSE version) uses a 30 cm bench — the original protocol uses 50 cm for men and 40 cm for women. The participant steps up and down for 5 minutes at a set pace. In the standard protocol the recovery pulse is measured in three 30-second windows (at 1:00–1:30, 2:00–2:30 and 3:00–3:30 after stopping); the GCSE-adapted version often takes a single reading from 1 minute post-exercise. A lower heart rate indicates a more efficient cardiovascular system. The fitness index is calculated and compared against normative data.

Agility, Strength, Muscular Endurance and Flexibility Tests

The Illinois agility run test measures agility. The participant starts lying face down and, on the signal, sprints up and back along a 10 m by 5 m rectangular course, weaving between four central cones spaced 3.3 metres apart. The time taken is recorded and compared against normative data. Shorter times indicate greater agility.

Grip strength is measured using a grip dynamometer. The participant squeezes the device as hard as possible; the result is recorded in kilograms and compared to normative tables.

Muscular endurance is assessed using one-minute tests. In the one-minute sit-up test, the participant performs as many full sit-ups as possible in 60 seconds with a partner holding their feet. In the one-minute press-up test, the participant performs as many full press-ups as possible in 60 seconds, maintaining correct form throughout. Higher numbers indicate greater muscular endurance.

Flexibility is measured using the sit and reach test. The participant sits with their legs straight against a measuring box, feet flat against the base, and reaches forward along the measuring scale as far as possible. The furthest point reached (in centimetres) is recorded. A greater score indicates greater lower back and hamstring flexibility.

Speed and Power Tests

The 30-metre sprint test measures speed. The participant sprints 30 metres from a standing start; the time is recorded using either a stopwatch or electronic timing gates. A lower time indicates greater speed. The vertical jump test measures power. The participant stands next to a wall, reaches up to mark their standing reach, then jumps as high as possible and touches the wall at the peak of the jump. The difference between the two marks, in centimetres, represents the jump height. A higher jump indicates greater leg power.

Key Fact

Test-to-component pairings: Cooper 12-minute run/swim → cardiovascular endurance; Harvard Step Test → cardiovascular endurance; Illinois agility run → agility; grip dynamometer → strength; one-minute sit-up/press-up → muscular endurance; 30 m sprint → speed; vertical jump → power; sit and reach → flexibility.

Normative data tables provide pre-established ranges of results for different age groups and genders. For example, a Cooper 12-minute run normative table might indicate that a 16-year-old male who covers 2,400 metres or more scores in the “excellent” category, while 1,800–2,000 metres is “below average.” Comparing an individual’s result to normative data tells the coach whether the performer is stronger or weaker than the population average in that component. It is important to use the correct normative table — age and gender must match, because expected results vary significantly between groups. Data interpretation questions in the exam will often ask you to compare a result to a provided table and draw a conclusion about the performer’s fitness level.

A common data task is calculating the percentage improvement between two test results. The formula is:

Percentage improvement = ((new score − original score) ÷ original score) × 100

Example: a student’s vertical jump improves from 40 cm to 47 cm after a 6-week plyometric programme. Percentage improvement = ((47 − 40) ÷ 40) × 100 = (7 ÷ 40) × 100 = 17.5%. Always show units in your final answer (in this case, %). Calculators are permitted in the written examination, but you still need to show your working clearly.

lessons.title: Principles of Training and Programme Design

before.content_html:
Why Principles Matter

Elite athletes do not train randomly. Their programmes are built on scientific principles that ensure each session produces the right adaptations without causing injury, boredom or wasted effort. Understanding these principles is essential for designing, evaluating and improving any training programme — whether for a school athlete, a club-level performer or a professional.

Individual Needs and Specificity

The first step in any programme is to assess the athlete’s individual needs. Individual needs recognises that no two athletes are the same. Age, fitness level, previous training history, current health status and the demands of the sport all vary. A 16-year-old beginner runner needs a very different programme from an experienced county-level distance runner of the same age.

Specificity means that training must replicate the demands of the sport. A sprinter must develop fast-twitch muscle fibres and the anaerobic energy system through short, explosive efforts — long, slow jogging would not produce the right adaptations. A swimmer must train in the water to develop sport-specific muscle recruitment patterns and technique under fatigue. If training is not specific, fitness gains will not transfer to improved performance.

Progressive Overload

Progressive overload states that the body only adapts when it is challenged beyond its current capacity. A load that was challenging four weeks ago will no longer produce adaptation once the body has adjusted to it. To continue improving, the athlete must progressively increase the training stimulus. This can be achieved by increasing frequency (training more days per week), intensity (working at a higher percentage of maximum heart rate or one rep max), time (training for longer durations) or type (introducing new and more demanding training methods). These four variables form the FITT framework.

Key Fact

FITT: Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard), Time (how long), Type (what method). All four variables can be manipulated to create progressive overload. For example, a runner could increase frequency from 3 to 4 sessions per week (frequency), run at 75% rather than 65% of maximum heart rate (intensity), extend sessions from 30 to 40 minutes (time), or add interval training alongside continuous runs (type).

Reversibility and Overtraining

Reversibility — sometimes called detraining — describes the loss of fitness adaptations when training stops. Cardiovascular fitness declines within 2–3 weeks of stopping aerobic training; muscular adaptations take longer to reverse but will decline with inactivity. Injury, illness and competition breaks all present reversibility risks. Athletes must plan rest carefully to avoid detraining while allowing recovery.

Overtraining is the opposite danger: pushing the body too hard without sufficient rest. Symptoms include persistent fatigue, declining performance, increased injury risk, mood changes and suppressed immune function. A well-designed programme builds overload gradually and includes planned rest and recovery phases.

Training Thresholds and Heart Rate Zones

To ensure training intensity is at the right level, coaches use training thresholds based on percentages of maximum heart rate. Maximum heart rate is estimated using the formula: maximum heart rate = 220 − age. For a 16-year-old, this gives 220 − 16 = 204 beats per minute (bpm).

The aerobic training zone sits between 60% and 80% of maximum heart rate. For a 16-year-old (max HR 204 bpm): lower boundary = 0.60 × 204 = 122 bpm; upper boundary = 0.80 × 204 = 163 bpm. Training within this zone develops cardiovascular endurance because the body is using oxygen efficiently to sustain effort.

The anaerobic training zone sits between 80% and 90% of maximum heart rate. For the same 16-year-old: lower boundary = 0.80 × 204 = 163 bpm; upper boundary = 0.90 × 204 = 184 bpm. At this intensity, the body cannot supply oxygen fast enough, so anaerobic pathways are used. Lactic acid accumulates, which limits duration. This zone develops speed, power and the ability to tolerate high-intensity effort.

Key Fact

Max HR formula: 220 − age. Aerobic zone: 60–80% of max HR (predominantly oxygen-based, builds cardiovascular endurance). Anaerobic zone: 80–90% of max HR (oxygen insufficient, builds speed/power, lactic acid produced). The boundaries are calculated by multiplying max HR by the decimal percentage.

A SMART target is a goal that is Specific (names the exact skill or component), Measurable (has a number), Achievable (within the athlete’s capacity), Realistic (appropriate to their current level) and Time-bound (has a deadline). A poorly written target is “I want to get better at running.” A well-written SMART target is: “I will improve my Cooper 12-minute run distance from 2,100 m to 2,300 m within 8 weeks of following my aerobic training programme.” This target names the test (specific and measurable), the improvement is within reach (achievable and realistic) and it has a deadline (time-bound). Mark schemes credit only targets that satisfy all five criteria simultaneously.

Students sometimes write that “progressive overload means working harder every session.” This risks overtraining. In reality, well-designed programmes build load progressively over several weeks, then include a ‘recovery week’ where volume drops before the next loading block begins. The key is that overload is introduced gradually and systematically over time, not relentlessly session by session. The body adapts during rest and recovery, not during the training stimulus itself — without adequate rest, the adaptations cannot occur and performance will stagnate or decline.
before.exam_tip_html: On Calculate questions involving training zones, always show three steps: (1) calculate max HR using 220 − age, (2) multiply max HR by the lower boundary percentage, (3) multiply max HR by the upper boundary percentage. Show the units (bpm) at each step. A common error is to apply the percentage directly to 220 rather than to the calculated max HR — this will give a wrong answer. For Explain questions on SMART targets, examiners expect all five criteria to be referenced, not just one or two. Write the target out in full and annotate which element satisfies each letter.

lessons.title: Methods of Training and Their Effects

before.exam_tip_html: A common error on training methods questions is stating a method without linking it to the specific fitness component or sport. “Circuit training is good for athletes” earns nothing; “circuit training develops muscular endurance and cardiovascular endurance, which are essential for a basketball player sustaining repeated explosive efforts across four quarters” earns full marks. For Discuss questions (4 marks), always present both advantages and disadvantages — mark schemes award half marks for one-sided answers. For Assess or Evaluate questions (6–9 marks), rank the methods and justify which is most appropriate for the given athlete or sport, using specific fitness component links and sporting examples throughout.

practice_questions.text:
Which training method involves alternating faster and slower effort periods over varied terrain without fixed rest intervals?
A) Continuous training
B) Circuit training
C) Fartlek training
D) Weight training
practice_questions.marks: C) Fartlek training [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'plyometric training'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for describing explosive/rapid movement; 1 mark for reference to the stretch-shortening cycle or the aim of developing power. Full definition: training that uses rapid explosive movements exploiting the stretch-shortening cycle of muscles to develop power.

practice_questions.text: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of using interval training to prepare a 16-year-old middle-distance runner for competition.
practice_questions.marks: Advantage (up to 2 marks): interval training allows the runner to work at a higher intensity than continuous training by including recovery periods (1); this develops both cardiovascular endurance and anaerobic capacity needed for the finishing kick in a race (1). Disadvantage (up to 2 marks): interval training is physically demanding and the risk of injury increases if recovery periods are too short (1); it requires careful monitoring to ensure the correct work-to-rest ratio for the runner's current fitness level (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how weight training can be adapted to develop either muscular strength or muscular endurance, using specific examples of how the load and repetitions would differ.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: for muscular strength, the athlete uses a heavy load (above 85% of 1RM) with low repetitions (1-6 reps) so the muscle is maximally overloaded in each set (1); for muscular endurance, a light load (below 65% of 1RM) with high repetitions (15+) keeps the muscle working under fatigue for an extended period (1).

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old county-level rugby player wants to improve her fitness over a 12-week pre-season block. Analyse which training methods would be most suitable for her sport and explain how they would be combined in a programme.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Fartlek training develops both aerobic base and speed, replicating the variable intensity of a rugby match (phases of sustained effort followed by sprints). Interval/HIIT develops anaerobic capacity needed for explosive tackles, scrums and sprints. Circuit training builds muscular endurance across whole-body movements relevant to rugby. Plyometrics develop the explosive power needed for jumping in lineouts or accelerating from stationary. A combined programme (e.g. fartlek twice weekly, circuit once, plyometrics once, with rest days) applies progressive overload by increasing intensity and duration week by week. Technically precise, consistent rugby application.

Secure: Identifies and justifies two or three methods with rugby application. Addresses combination.

Developing: Names methods without full application. Some connection to rugby.

Emerging: Names one method. No combination addressed.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether plyometric training or continuous training would be more beneficial for a club-level 100m sprinter. Use the principles of training to support your judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: For plyometrics — develops power through the stretch-shortening cycle; directly relevant to the explosive start and acceleration phase of a 100m race; satisfies specificity (explosive power is the primary demand). For continuous training — develops cardiovascular endurance, which helps with recovery between training sessions and warm-down; however, a 100m race is approximately 10 seconds and predominantly anaerobic, so cardiovascular endurance is not the limiting factor in race performance. Conclusion: plyometric training is more directly beneficial to the sprinter's event-specific performance; continuous training plays a supportive role in general conditioning but should not dominate the programme. References overtraining (mixing methods avoids repetitive strain), progressive overload (plyometric load increases across the programme). Balanced, applies principles, firm conclusion.

Secure: Argues both methods with sprinting application. Principles referenced. Reaches conclusion.

Developing: Focuses more on one method. Some sporting application.

Emerging: Describes one method. No evaluation.

lessons.title: Injury Prevention, PARQ, RICE and PEDs

before.content_html:
Preventing Injury Before It Happens

Injury is one of the biggest barriers to consistent training and performance. Preventing injury requires a proactive approach: screening individuals before they train, applying the principles of training correctly to avoid overuse, using appropriate equipment, and following the rules of the activity. When injury does occur, the correct immediate treatment limits damage and speeds recovery.

The PARQ: Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire

Before starting a new training programme, an individual should complete a PARQ (Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire). The PARQ is a short set of questions asking about cardiovascular health, recent illness, known medical conditions, bone or joint problems, pregnancy, prescription medication and any other reasons that might make vigorous exercise unsuitable without medical guidance. If a person answers “yes” to any question, they are advised to consult a doctor before beginning training. The PARQ protects both the individual and the coach — it ensures that exercise is safe and that any training programme is adapted to the person’s health status.

Injury Prevention Strategies

Applying the principles of training correctly is the first line of defence against overuse injuries. Increasing training load too quickly — violating progressive overload — is the single most common cause of overuse injury in sport. Shin splints, stress fractures and tendinopathy all develop when training volume or intensity increases faster than the body can adapt. A structured programme with planned rest and recovery prevents this.

Additional prevention strategies include: following the rules of the activity to minimise contact injuries; using appropriate protective clothing and equipment (helmets, shin pads, gum shields, braces); and checking facilities and equipment before use to remove hazards such as uneven surfaces, damaged apparatus or unsuitable footwear.

Common Injuries in Sport

Several injury types appear on the specification. Concussion is a traumatic brain injury caused by a blow to the head. Symptoms include headache, confusion, dizziness and nausea. Any athlete suspected of concussion must be removed from play immediately and not return until medically cleared — the “if in doubt, sit them out” protocol. Fractures are breaks in bone. A dislocation occurs when joint surfaces are forced out of alignment, commonly at the shoulder or finger. A sprain is damage to a ligament at a joint; a strain is damage to a muscle or tendon. Torn cartilage, most commonly the meniscus of the knee, occurs when the fibrocartilage cushion is twisted under load. Soft tissue injuries also include tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis), golfer’s elbow (medial epicondylitis) and abrasions (skin surface injuries from friction).

Key Fact

RICE is the immediate treatment protocol for soft tissue injuries: Rest (stop activity to prevent further damage), Ice (apply for 15–20 minutes to reduce swelling and pain), Compression (bandage to limit swelling), Elevation (raise the injured part above heart level to reduce blood pooling). RICE is applied in the first 24–48 hours after injury.

Key Fact

Seven banned PED categories: anabolic steroids (strength/power), EPO and blood doping (endurance oxygen), growth hormones (muscle mass/fat loss), stimulants (alertness/endurance), narcotic analgesics (pain masking), diuretics (weight loss/masking), beta blockers (precision steadiness). All are banned under WADA rules.

Performance-Enhancing Drugs (PEDs)

Performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs) are substances used to gain an unfair advantage in sport. They are banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) and their use is considered cheating. Each category of PED has specific effects and health risks.

Anabolic steroids are synthetic versions of testosterone. They increase muscle protein synthesis, leading to greater muscle hypertrophy, strength and recovery. They are used in power and strength sports. Health risks include liver damage, cardiovascular disease, hormonal disruption (including reduced fertility), aggression and, in young athletes, early closure of growth plates. Beta blockers reduce heart rate and control tremors. They are used in precision sports such as archery, shooting and snooker. Health risks include lowered blood pressure and bradycardia.

Stimulants increase alertness, concentration and aggression, and delay the onset of fatigue. They include amphetamines and some substances found in cold remedies. Health risks include elevated heart rate, anxiety, cardiac arrhythmia and addiction. Narcotic analgesics are powerful painkillers that allow athletes to compete through injuries that would otherwise force them to stop. They carry risks of addiction, impaired judgement and masking damage that could worsen without rest.

Erythropoietin (EPO) is a peptide hormone that stimulates the bone marrow to produce more red blood cells, increasing the blood’s oxygen-carrying capacity. This improves aerobic endurance significantly and is used in cycling, marathon running and cross-country skiing. The health risks are severe: increased blood viscosity raises the risk of blood clots, stroke and heart attack. Growth hormones (GH) stimulate muscle growth and fat loss. Health risks include abnormal bone and organ growth (acromegaly) and joint pain. Diuretics increase urine production. They are used either to achieve rapid weight loss for weight-category sports (boxing, judo) or to dilute urine samples in an attempt to hide other banned substances. Health risks include severe dehydration and electrolyte imbalance. Blood doping involves removing an athlete’s blood, storing it, then re-infusing it before competition to raise red blood cell count. Like EPO, it increases oxygen-carrying capacity and carries similar cardiovascular risks.

PEDs damage sport in two ways: ethically and physically. Ethically, they violate the principles of fair competition — athletes who dope gain an advantage unavailable to those who train within the rules, making meaningful competition impossible. They undermine the values of honesty, integrity and respect that form the foundation of sport. For young athletes, doping also creates a coercive culture: if some competitors dope, those who do not risk being left behind, placing athletes in an unfair dilemma. Physically, every category of PED carries documented health risks. The severity ranges from addiction and cardiovascular disease to potentially fatal blood clotting events associated with EPO and blood doping. Anti-doping testing (urine and blood samples) and biological passport programmes aim to detect PED use and protect the integrity of competition.

A sprain involves a ligament (the tissue connecting bone to bone at a joint). A strain involves a muscle or tendon (the tissue connecting muscle to bone). The confusion arises because both present with pain, swelling and localised bruising. The key question is: where is the damage? A twisted ankle with pain on the outer side of the joint is likely a lateral ligament sprain. A hamstring tear from sprinting is a strain of the muscle belly. Both are treated initially with RICE, but recovery timelines and rehabilitation differ. In the exam, using the wrong term will lose marks — always identify whether the damaged tissue is a ligament or a muscle/tendon.

lessons.title: Using Data in Physical Activity and Sport

before.content_html:
Why Data Matters in Sport

Modern sport is driven by data. Premier League clubs analyse thousands of data points per match to inform selection and tactics. Olympic coaches monitor heart rate, lactate thresholds and power outputs to fine-tune training loads. Even at school level, recording fitness test results and tracking improvement over time transforms vague feelings of “getting fitter” into evidence-based decisions. Understanding how to collect, present and interpret data is a core skill embedded throughout the written examination — data questions appear in every section, not just a dedicated data topic.

Qualitative and Quantitative Data

All data in sport falls into one of two broad categories. Quantitative data deals with numbers and measurements. Heart rate in beats per minute, sprint time in seconds, vertical jump height in centimetres, percentage body fat — these are all quantitative because they give a numerical value that can be compared against norms or tracked over time. Quantitative data can be collected using instruments (stopwatches, heart rate monitors, dynamometers) and analysed statistically.

Qualitative data, by contrast, deals with descriptions, observations and judgements. A coach writing that a swimmer’s stroke technique “lacks rotation at the hip” is providing qualitative data. An athlete’s self-reported motivation level (“I feel more confident since starting the programme”) is qualitative. Qualitative data provides rich, contextual information that numbers alone cannot capture, but it is harder to compare objectively.

Key Fact

Quantitative data = numbers (e.g. Cooper run distance: 2,400 m; press-ups per minute: 32). Qualitative data = descriptions (e.g. “the athlete’s technique improved significantly over the block”). Both types are used in sport, often together: a coach uses quantitative fitness test scores alongside qualitative observation of movement quality.

Presenting Data: Tables and Graphs

Raw data is difficult to interpret on its own. Presenting data in a table or graph reveals patterns, trends and comparisons that would be missed in a list of numbers. Tables are useful for displaying exact values across multiple variables (e.g. fitness test results for a group of athletes across three testing sessions). Each column should have a clear heading and units stated (bpm, seconds, cm, %).

Graphs allow visual comparison of trends over time or between groups. A bar chart is suitable for comparing discrete categories (e.g. the number of students achieving each fitness category in a class). A line graph shows change over time (e.g. a swimmer’s 100 m time improving over a season) and is appropriate when data points are connected by a continuous trend. A pie chart is suited to showing proportions (e.g. the percentage of total training time spent in each heart rate zone). Choosing the wrong graph type for the data loses marks in the exam.

Interpreting Data Against Normative Tables

Once collected, individual results are compared against normative data tables to evaluate performance. A normative table for the Cooper 12-minute run might categorise results for 16-year-old males as: Excellent (>2,800 m), Above Average (2,400–2,800 m), Average (2,000–2,400 m), Below Average (1,600–2,000 m), Poor (<1,600 m). An athlete who runs 2,550 m can therefore be placed in the “Above Average” category for their age group.

Interpreting data accurately requires three steps: quote the relevant figure with its unit; compare it to a reference point (the normative category, a personal best or another athlete’s score); and state the sporting or training implication. Missing any one of these three steps reduces the marks available.

Percentage change is one of the most frequently tested data calculations. The formula is:

Percentage change = ((new value − original value) ÷ original value) × 100

Example: a hockey player’s Illinois agility run time improves from 17.4 seconds to 15.9 seconds after an 8-week agility programme. Percentage improvement = ((17.4 − 15.9) ÷ 17.4) × 100 = (1.5 ÷ 17.4) × 100 = 8.6%. Note that for time-based tests, a lower score is better (the “improvement” is a reduction). Always show your working: state the formula, substitute the numbers, calculate, then state the final answer with units (%). Calculators are permitted in the written examination.

When describing a trend in a graph or table, students often lose marks by identifying the trend without supporting it with a number. The examiner wants: (1) the trend (“cardiovascular endurance improved over the 12-week programme”), (2) a quoted figure with units (“the Cooper run score increased from 2,100 m to 2,450 m”), and (3) a conclusion (“this suggests the continuous training programme was effective at developing aerobic fitness”). A conclusion about a decline should also address potential causes — if a score dropped in week 8, consider whether this coincided with increased training load (overtraining) or illness. Always read the full data set before drawing a conclusion about a single data point.

Key Fact

Three steps for data interpretation: (1) quote the figure with units; (2) compare to a reference point (norm, personal best or another result); (3) state the implication for training or performance. Percentage change formula: ((new − original) ÷ original) × 100. Always state units in the answer.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of quantitative data collected during a fitness testing session?
A) The coach's observation that the athlete's technique improved
B) The athlete's self-reported confidence level
C) The athlete's vertical jump height measured in centimetres
D) A written description of the athlete's warm-up routine
practice_questions.marks: C) The athlete's vertical jump height measured in centimetres [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'qualitative data' and give one example from physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for definition: data expressed in descriptions, observations or opinions rather than numbers; 1 mark for a valid example from physical activity (e.g. a coach's written assessment of an athlete's technique, or an athlete's self-reported motivation level).

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows a 16-year-old athlete's Cooper 12-minute run results over three testing sessions.

Session | Date        | Distance (m)
1       | September   | 2,050
2       | November    | 2,240
3       | January     | 2,410

Calculate the percentage improvement in Cooper run distance between Session 1 and Session 3.
practice_questions.marks: Formula: ((new - original) / original) x 100 (1 mark for correct formula or working); = ((2,410 - 2,050) / 2,050) x 100 = (360 / 2,050) x 100 = 17.6% (1 mark for correct calculation); 17.6% improvement (1 mark for correct answer with % sign and clear statement of improvement).

practice_questions.text: Using the data in Table 1 above, interpret what the results suggest about the effectiveness of the athlete's training programme between September and January.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: the Cooper run distance increased from 2,050 m in September to 2,410 m in January (1 mark for quoting specific figures with units); this represents a consistent upward trend across all three sessions, with an improvement of approximately 360 m over the period (1 mark for identifying the trend); the rate of improvement was similar between Session 1 to 2 (190 m) and Session 2 to 3 (170 m), suggesting a steady training effect (1 mark for comparing sub-periods or noting consistency); this indicates that the training programme was effective at developing cardiovascular endurance (1 mark for a valid training implication).

practice_questions.text:
A sports coach has been monitoring four athletes' press-up test scores over a 10-week training block. The results are shown below.

Athlete | Week 1 score | Week 10 score
Tara    | 22           | 29
Marcus  | 18           | 26
Lucy    | 30           | 35
Ben     | 14           | 20

Analyse the data to identify which athlete made the greatest relative improvement and explain what this tells the coach about the training block.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correctly calculates percentage improvement for each athlete: Tara: (29-22)/22 x 100 = 31.8%; Marcus: (26-18)/18 x 100 = 44.4%; Lucy: (35-30)/30 x 100 = 16.7%; Ben: (20-14)/14 x 100 = 42.9%. Identifies Marcus as the greatest relative improver at 44.4%. Notes that Ben's absolute improvement (6 press-ups) is the same as Marcus's but Ben's relative improvement is 42.9% due to a lower starting point. Discusses what this tells the coach: the training block was effective for all athletes in developing muscular endurance; athletes starting from a lower baseline (Marcus, Ben) tend to show greater relative gains (principle of initial fitness level / diminishing returns); Lucy's lower percentage gain from a higher base is typical of athletes already nearer their ceiling. Technically precise throughout.

Secure: Correctly identifies greatest relative improver with a percentage calculation. Provides training implication. Mostly accurate.

Developing: Calculates some percentages. Partial analysis of implications.

Emerging: Notes an improvement without calculation. Basic observation only.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of using normative data when interpreting fitness test results for a group of 16-year-old athletes preparing for regional competition.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: For — normative data provides a standardised reference against which individual results can be categorised (excellent, above average, etc.), making individual scores meaningful; it allows the coach to identify which athletes are performing above or below the expected level for their age and gender, directing targeted training; it enables goal-setting (e.g. moving from average to above average in 8 weeks); over time, tracking results against norms monitors whether the training programme is effective. Against — limitations of normative data: normative tables are typically based on large population samples that may not reflect elite regional competition standards; the tables may be outdated if they pre-date changes in typical fitness levels; normative data does not account for individual variation, injury history or positional demands within a team sport. Conclusion: normative data is a valuable benchmarking tool but must be supplemented with sport-specific standards and individual performance history for athletes competing at regional level. Balanced, applied to 16-year-old athletes, concluded.

Secure: Identifies benefits and at least one limitation. Application to athletes present. Attempted conclusion.

Developing: Discusses benefits or limitations but not both. Some sporting application.

Emerging: States that normative data compares results. No evaluation.
